category: kabbalistic treatise (on the sefirot and divine emanation)

date.note: Composed in 1292 (some scholarship gives 1292-1293) in Castile, on the dating accepted in the scholarship (Scholem; the critical edition by Mopsik). It is one of the Hebrew works Moses de Leon wrote under his own name.

summary: Shekel ha-Kodesh ('the Sacred Shekel'), composed by the Castilian kabbalist Moses de Leon in 1292, is a Hebrew treatise on the ten sefirot and the divine emanation. It is one of the works de Leon wrote under his own name, distinct from the Zohar that modern scholarship attributes to him, and it is of particular interest to scholars because it cites Zoharic passages, which bears on the study of the Zohar's formation. It was critically edited by Charles Mopsik, with an introduction by Moshe Idel (Cherub Press, 1996), and an earlier Hebrew edition was published by A. W. Greenup (London, 1911).
description:
Shekel ha-Kodesh (the 'Sacred Shekel', a term drawn from the sanctuary weight of the Torah) is a Hebrew kabbalistic treatise composed by Moses ben Shem Tov de Leon (c. 1240-1305) in Castile in 1292. Like Sefer ha-Rimmon, it is one of the works de Leon wrote and circulated under his own name, and its authorship, unlike that of the Zohar, is not in dispute.

The treatise expounds the kabbalistic theosophy of its time and place: the doctrine of the ten sefirot, the emanated divine potencies through which, in kabbalistic teaching, God acts and becomes knowable, and the process of divine emanation from the hidden Ein Sof. In the scholarship the work has a particular evidentiary importance for the study of the Zohar, because de Leon quotes in it passages of Zoharic character, including material whose relation to the known Zoharic corpus is examined by scholars; the correspondence between his signed Hebrew works and the Aramaic Zohar is central to the argument, made in detail by Gershom Scholem, that de Leon composed the bulk of the Zohar. On that account the signed treatises and the pseudepigraphic Zohar issue from the same hand in late-thirteenth-century Castile; the attribution of the Zohar to de Leon is recorded here as the academic position within the unadjudicated dispute over the Zohar's authorship, alongside the traditional ascription to the second-century Shimon bar Yochai, exactly as in the moses-de-leon and zohar entries.

Shekel ha-Kodesh survives and has been edited more than once: an early edition of the Hebrew text was published by A. W. Greenup (London, 1911), and a critical edition was prepared by Charles Mopsik, with an introduction by Moshe Idel, in the series Sources and Studies in the Literature of Jewish Mysticism (Cherub Press, 1996). This entry presents the work on the tradition's own terms as a kabbalistic treatise on the sefirot and divine emanation and records the scholarly account of its authorship, its date, and its bearing on the study of the Zohar.
